power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Interpersonal connection emerges through conversation.
Theories of interpersonal communication hold that conversational partners increasingly align in how they express meaning, build on one another's contributions, and experience connection.
Yet how such alignment unfolds during a conversation, and how it relates to the experience of a "good" interaction, remains largely untested.
Seventy dyads of previously unacquainted individuals held naturalistic conversations while dual functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) recorded neural activity.
We measured semantic alignment using convergence entropy and substantive exchange, the number of adjacent turns in which both partners contributed contentful talk.
Contrary to a convergence account, dyads broadened their semantic range over time.
Subjective experience was predicted not by semantic alignment but by substantive exchange, particularly in shallow-prompt conversations.
Neurally, inter-brain synchrony tracked substantive exchange, whereas semantic alignment was reflected in partners' matched turn-to-turn neural dynamics.
First conversations build connection through reciprocal, substantive exchange, with distinct linguistic and neural signatures.
Building Connection Through Conversation:

text.text: Whereas the field of interpersonal communication has heavily relied on monadic, summative, and self-report data to draw inferences about conversations, support for BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 4 theoretical claims is strengthened by analysis of dyadic, intensive longitudinal, and multimodal data.
In this study, we investigate the emergence of semantic alignment in initial conversations between previously unacquainted strangers.

Specifically, we draw on communication accommodation theory (Giles et al., 1991), a dynamic dyadic systems perspective on interpersonal communication (Solomon et al., 2021 (Solomon et al., , 2023)), and the process model of creating understanding (Gasiorek & Aune, 2021) to develop hypotheses about the form, neurobiological underpinnings, and outcomes of getting-to-know-you conversations.
text.formatted: Specifically, we draw on communication accommodation theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Giles et al., 1991)</ref>, a dynamic dyadic systems perspective on interpersonal communication <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Solomon et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Solomon et al., , 2023))</ref>, and the process model of creating understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gasiorek & Aune, 2021)</ref> to develop hypotheses about the form, neurobiological underpinnings, and outcomes of getting-to-know-you conversations.

text.text: Building on these perspectives, we incorporate advances in computational methods and social neuroscience in our tests.
In what follows, we elaborate on the theories and methods that informed this project.

Communication accommodation theory (CAT) conceptualizes convergence as the tendency for interactants to adapt their communicative behaviors toward one another in order to manage social distance and shared identity (Giles et al., 1991; Soliz et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Communication accommodation theory (CAT) conceptualizes convergence as the tendency for interactants to adapt their communicative behaviors toward one another in order to manage social distance and shared identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Giles et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Soliz et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Empirically, linguistic convergence has been observed across a wide range of communicative features, including lexical choice, syntactic structure, stylistic markers, and semantic framing (Branigan et al., 2000; Pickering & Garrod, 2004; Tausczik & Pennebaker, 2010).

text.text: These adaptations are not limited to surface-level mimicry; speakers also converge at the level of meaning, progressively aligning on conceptual structures and shared interpretations of conversational topics (Bradac et al., 1988; Doyle et al., 2017; Dragojevic & Giles, 2014).

text.text: From a dyadic perspective, convergence reflects an increasingly interdependent system in which each speaker's contributions are shaped by-and predictive of-the other's speech.

As shared understanding increases, interlocutors become more capable of anticipating how their partner will talk about a given topic, indicating greater mutual information in the way meaning is jointly constructed over time.
Complementing CAT, the present study adopts a dynamic dyadic systems (DDS) perspective on interpersonal communication (Solomon et al., 2021 (Solomon et al., , 2023)).
text.formatted: Complementing CAT, the present study adopts a dynamic dyadic systems (DDS) perspective on interpersonal communication <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Solomon et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Solomon et al., , 2023))</ref>.

text.text: Recognizing that individuals in conversation are simultaneously autonomous and interdependent actors, the DDS perspective treats conversation as a dynamic system that manifests qualities like selforganization and self-stabilization; as a dyadic system, the trajectory of interaction takes shape in the exchange of speaking turns between interactants.

By tracking the multimodal dynamics constructed by dyad members in an interaction, the DDS perspective privileges the emergent qualities and phase shifts in conversation, such as the alignment of meaning in dialogue.
From this perspective, semantic alignment and substantive exchange are distinct signatures of a dyadic system.
Semantic alignment is a property of the exchanged turns, concerning how closely the meaning expressed by one partner relates to what the other has just contributed in the adjacent turn.
Substantive exchange, by contrast, focuses on the accumulation of reciprocal participation, referring to how often both partners contribute contentful talk across adjacent turns.
These properties need not vary together.
Partners may sustain extensive back-and-forth while continually introducing new meanings, or remain closely aligned in meaning across relatively few substantive exchanges.

Because interactional systems are constituted through repeated exchanges between partners, we therefore treat the amount of substantive exchange as a feature of the dyadic interaction in its own right, alongside semantic alignment.

Further, the process model of creating understanding describes the emergence and functions of alignment in interaction (Gasiorek & Aune, 2021). Gasiorek and Aune (2021) noted the limitations in a conventional, code-based model of communication (i.e., meanings are encoded into and decoded from specific signals).

text.text: Rather, interaction is viewed as a process of aligning situation models between interlocutors through the presentation of stimuli and activation BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 6 of meme states.

Individuals are motivated to align their situation models because the accomplishment of social goals hinges upon the creation of understanding, and humans display an inherent social orientation that drives attempts at seeking alignment.

This theoretical process implicates predictive inference-making as a key step in creating understanding: individuals venture informed guesses about what comes next in the conversation, and this activity provides an ongoing basis for evaluating and correcting the situation model of the interaction.

Further, as generating predictions and responding to a conversation partner are cognitive activities that require computational resources, the process of interactive alignment is constrained by a disposition toward efficiency.
These assumptions about the process of alignment, in turn, manifest patterns of entrainment in neurobiological markers between interactants during a conversation.
Recent work has increasingly framed convergence in explicitly information-theoretic terms, emphasizing predictability, redundancy, and incremental novelty in conversational dynamics.

Speaking turns typically introduce new information relative to the immediately preceding context, while simultaneously preserving and building upon stable shared meanings established earlier in the interaction (Enfield, 2017).
text.formatted: Speaking turns typically introduce new information relative to the immediately preceding context, while simultaneously preserving and building upon stable shared meanings established earlier in the interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Enfield, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Skilled conversationalists are perceived as such not because they maximize novelty, but because they introduce just enough new information while maintaining coherence with prior turns.

Convergence entropy formalizes this balance by quantifying how much uncertainty remains in one speaker's verbal-semantic contributions given a conversation partner's prior verbal behavior (Rosen & Dale, 2023).
text.formatted: Convergence entropy formalizes this balance by quantifying how much uncertainty remains in one speaker's verbal-semantic contributions given a conversation partner's prior verbal behavior <ref type="bibr">(Rosen & Dale, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Lower convergence entropy indicates a more tightly coupled dyadic system in which meaning unfolds predictably yet flexibly, reducing the degrees of freedom interlocutors must manage during coordination (Kelso, 1994; Riley et al., 2011).

text.text: Importantly, such alignment has been repeatedly BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 7 linked to smoother interaction, greater interpersonal affiliation, and more successful joint action (Dale et al., 2013; Soliz et al., 2021; Gasiorek & Aune, 2021).
text.formatted: Importantly, such alignment has been repeatedly BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 7 linked to smoother interaction, greater interpersonal affiliation, and more successful joint action <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dale et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Soliz et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gasiorek & Aune, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, the research reviewed thus far poses contradicting predictions with regard to how entropy changes over the course of an interaction.
The accommodation and alignment framework implies that as partners converge, adjacent turns should become progressively more predictable from one another, resulting in decrease in entropy.

The information-exchange account implies the opposite trajectory: as strangers get to know each other, they would strive to maximize novelty while maintaining alignment, hence conversational turns should carry progressively more new information, signaled by an increase in entropy.
A getting-to-know-you conversation is thus a suitable context to examine this theoretical debate.

In this way, convergence entropy provides a principled bridge between classic communication theories of accommodation and contemporary computational approaches to modeling meaning-making as an emergent, dyadic process.
In addition to documenting the pattern of change in semantic alignment, an aim of this investigation was to examine the neurobiological underpinnings of these changes.

These turn-byturn processes of meaning-making are supported not only by the core language network in the brain, but also by broader neural systems involved in social, contextual, and internally oriented cognition (Zada et al., 2026).

text.text: In this regard, the default mode network (DMN) might play a key role in processes that extend beyond the language-selective system, such as introspection, selfreflection, and the construction of mental narratives (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014).

text.text: Not a specialized linguistic network, the DMN functions as an active and dynamic sense-making network, integrating incoming external information with internally generated knowledge to construct a coherent situational model of the interaction (Fedorenko et al., 2024; Yeshurun et al., BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 8 2021).

text.text: Its long temporal receptive window enables it to track discourse-level structure, such as relationships across sentences and narrative segments, more robustly than the language network alone (e.g., Hasson et al., 2015; Lerner et al., 2011).

text.text: Prior work shows that DMN regions are recruited more strongly for coherent discourse than for disconnected sentences and can integrate information across multiple sentences and conversational turns (Yeshurun et al., 2017).

text.text: As a result, the DMN may also contribute to interpreting linguistic meaning at a higher level.
For example, extracting global themes, maintaining context, or linking incoming utterances to prior knowledge.

This joint operation of the language network and DMN suggests that understanding discourse requires not only linguistic decoding but also the domain-general processes that support continuity, integration, and contextual interpretation in communication.
The default mode network (DMN) is centrally involved in the internally oriented processes that support meaningful interpersonal connection.

DMN regions are activated when people reflect on their own beliefs, values, autobiographical memories, and future plans (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014; Buckner & Carroll, 2007), and when they juxtapose another person's experiences with their own to construct a shared or comparable mental landscape (Gasiorek & Aune, 2021).

text.text: During social interaction, this comparison process is essential: understanding another's disclosures requires mapping them onto one's own life history, evaluating their relevance, and anticipating likely future behaviors or intentions-all computations supported by the DMN's integrative architecture and long temporal receptive windows (Yeshurun et al., 2021).

text.text: Accordingly, DMN activity increases during conversations that demand greater interpersonal perspective-taking, such as deep, self-disclosing, or emotionally rich exchanges, and during interactions that elicit stronger social bonding (e.g., Paunov et al., 2019; Stephens et al., 2010).

text.text: These findings suggest that DMN engagement reflects the cognitive work BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 9 of constructing high-level relational meaning: the more an interaction requires aligning one's internal models with another's lived experience, the greater the recruitment of DMN systems, and the stronger the resulting sense of connection.
Interpersonal neural coordination, however, can take different forms.

Inter-brain synchrony (IBS) asks whether two people's neural signals rise and fall together in time, and the strongest IBS finding from this dataset lies in DMN and predicted connection between partners (Miao et al., 2026).

text.text: Complexity matching, on the other hand, asks whether two people's signals fluctuate by similar amount at a given timescale, without time-locking the specific fluctuations (Abney et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Complexity matching, on the other hand, asks whether two people's signals fluctuate by similar amount at a given timescale, without time-locking the specific fluctuations <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abney et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Two partners can be closely matched in the magnitude of their turn-to-turn (i.e. several seconds) neural variability without their signals peaking at the same moment.

If meaning construction in conversation is jointly contributed across alternating speaker and listener roles, successful experience may register less as simultaneous co-activation and more as partners' neural dynamics gradually resembling one another, reflecting as an interpersonal synergy (Fusaroli & Tylén, 2016).

text.text: Distinguishing these two forms of coordination allows us to ask not only whether brains track conversation, but also which facet of conversation each form of coordination tracks.

The study included 140 individuals who formed 70 dyads of previously unacquainted participants (20 male-male, 24 female-female, 23 male-female, two male-other, and one femaleother).
Participants were recruited from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) Departments of Psychology and Communication subject pools, as well as through flyers posted on campus.
All participants self-reported English as their primary language.
Experimental procedures were approved by the UCLA Institutional Review Board (IRB #22-001209), and all participants provided informed consent prior to participation.
The study employed a between-dyads experimental design with two conversation conditions: shallow and deep.

The shallow condition included 10 male-male, 13 female-female, BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 11 11 male-female, and two male-other dyads, and the deep condition included 10 male-male, 11 female-female, 12 male-female, and one female-other dyad.
Each experimental session involved two strangers engaging in a face-to-face, get-toknow-you conversation.
Conversation prompts were displayed sequentially on a shared computer screen and consisted of either shallow or deep topics (see Table 1), adapted from Kardas and colleagues (2022).
text.formatted: Conversation prompts were displayed sequentially on a shared computer screen and consisted of either shallow or deep topics (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>), adapted from <ref type="bibr">Kardas and colleagues (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Prompts appeared in a fixed order for all dyads.
Participants read each prompt simultaneously and volunteered to respond in the order they preferred.
They were instructed to remain on topic, take as much time as needed for each prompt, and advance to the next prompt by pressing a button once they had finished discussing the current topic.
During the conversation, both participants wore functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) caps to allow for simultaneous measurement of neural activity (Figure 1).
text.formatted: During the conversation, both participants wore functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) caps to allow for simultaneous measurement of neural activity (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: The interaction was audiovisually recorded to enable subsequent linguistic analyses.
No experimenter was present in the room during the conversation.
Each conversational session lasted approximately 20 minutes.
Following the conversation, participants completed a series of questionnaires assessing subjective experiences of the interaction.
Immediately following the conversation, participants rated their subjective experiences of the interaction on five-point scales.

Analyses in this article focus on these items: perceived conversational depth ("How deep did YOU feel the conversation went?") (M = 2.59, SD = 0.71), engagement ("How engaging did YOU find the conversation content?") (M = 3.75, SD = 0.63), similarity ("How similar do YOU think you and your partner are?") (M = 2.95, SD = 0.72), liking ("How much did YOU like your conversation partner?") (M = 3.94, SD = 0.51), and BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 12 friendship potential ("How likely do YOU think the two of you could become friends in the real world?") (M = 3.17, SD = 0.60).
Several methods have been developed to measure linguistic convergence, or the extent to which conversation partners become aligned in their language use (Giles et al., 2023; Duran et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Several methods have been developed to measure linguistic convergence, or the extent to which conversation partners become aligned in their language use <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Giles et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Duran et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We measured linguistic convergence using Convergence Entropy (CE), an information-theoretic approach developed by Rosen and Dale (2023).
text.formatted: We measured linguistic convergence using Convergence Entropy (CE), an information-theoretic approach developed by <ref type="bibr">Rosen and Dale (2023)</ref>.

text.text: Leveraging transformer language models, CE quantifies how predictable the semantic content of one speaker's turn is from the other speaker's preceding turn.

In this framework, lower CE values indicate greater linguistic alignment, and higher values indicate that a turn is less semantically predictable from the preceding turn and therefore introduces more new semantic information.

Linguistic data preprocessing steps included extracting audio files from the video record of each interaction, transcribing with an automated speech-to-text system (Otter.ai), and verifying across multiple rounds of manual correction by trained research assistants.
The preprocessed transcripts were segmented into conversational turns, defined as continuous stretches of speech by one speaker until the other began.
Each turn was time-stamped at the onset of its first word.

To calculate CE scores, transcripts were processed with RoBERTa, a transformer language model that represents words and word fragments (i.e. tokens) as numerical vectors capturing their semantic context.
These vectors were then used to compute CE for every crossspeaker turn pair, indicating linguistic alignment of two conversation partners on a turn-by-turn level.

Since raw CE values are strongly affected by how long a turn is, all analyses below use corrected entropy values adjusted for turn length (referred to hereafter as "entropy"), so that BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 13 longer utterances did not automatically produce higher entropy values.
For dyad-level analyses, entropy values were averaged across the conversation to index each dyad's overall level of semantic alignment.
Further explanations of the CE method and details of this adjustment are provided in Supplemental Materials.
Because all conversations were designed to last approximately 20 minutes, we devised a measure to capture how dyads use that conversation time.
To isolate reciprocal and contentful exchanges, we adopted the five-token threshold recommended by Rosen and Dale (2023) for statistically reliable entropy estimation.
text.formatted: To isolate reciprocal and contentful exchanges, we adopted the five-token threshold recommended by <ref type="bibr">Rosen and Dale (2023)</ref> for statistically reliable entropy estimation.

text.text: We defined a "substantive exchange" as an adjacent turn pair in which both speakers produced at least five tokens.
This is a quantitative way to capture portions of conversation in which both speakers contributed sufficient linguistic content for their adjacent turns to be meaningfully compared.

Neural activity was recorded simultaneously from both conversation partners using a mobile functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) system, with 40 measurement channels providing partial cortical coverage of four brain networks: the default mode network (DMN), the frontoparietal network (FPN), the ventral attention network (VAN), and the dorsal attention network (DAN; Figure 2).
text.formatted: Neural activity was recorded simultaneously from both conversation partners using a mobile functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) system, with 40 measurement channels providing partial cortical coverage of four brain networks: the default mode network (DMN), the frontoparietal network (FPN), the ventral attention network (VAN), and the dorsal attention network (DAN; Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Our hypotheses concern the DMN; the FPN, VAN, and DAN were examined without a priori predictions.

Neural data preprocessing steps followed the standardized pipeline reported in Miao et al. (2026), including addressing low-quality channels, motion artifacts, cardiac, respiratory, drift components, among other steps.
text.formatted: Neural data preprocessing steps followed the standardized pipeline reported in <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Miao et al. (2026)</ref>, including addressing low-quality channels, motion artifacts, cardiac, respiratory, drift components, among other steps.

text.text: Measurements that did not meet predefined quality thresholds were treated as missing.
As a result, usable network-level data were available for 69 dyads for the DMN, 69 for the FPN, 70 for the VAN, and 49 for the DAN.
Two complementary measures of interpersonal neural coordination were examined.

First, we used previously computed inter-brain synchrony (IBS) values from Miao et al. (2026), which quantify the extent to which partners' neural time series rise and fall together over the conversation with time-locked Pearson correlations.
text.formatted: First, we used previously computed inter-brain synchrony (IBS) values from <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Miao et al. (2026)</ref>, which quantify the extent to which partners' neural time series rise and fall together over the conversation with time-locked Pearson correlations.

text.text: In addition to the four network-level groupings described above, the same 40 channels were also grouped into seven anatomically defined regions: medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), left and right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (l-dlPFC and r-dlPFC), left and right temporoparietal junction (lTPJ and rTPJ), and left and right superior parietal lobule (lSPL and rSPL).
IBS values were available at both the network and anatomical-region levels.
The present study reused these existing values to examine their relationship with linguistic behavior.

Second, using the preprocessed channel-wise neural data, we characterized the dynamics of each participant's neural activity using Allan variance (AVAR), and compared partners at the timescale of conversational turn following the logic of complexity matching research, which compares the temporal organization of two interacting systems (Abney et al., 2014 (Abney et al., , 2021;; Rigoli et al., 2020).

text.text: Complexity matching has also been applied to neural data (Harrison et al., 2018; Carpentier et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Complexity matching has also been applied to neural data <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Harrison et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Carpentier et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Whereas conventional complexity matching compares dynamics across multiple timescales, we focused specifically on the timescale of conversational turns to align the neural analysis with our turn-level linguistic measures.

At the turn scale, AVAR captures how much a participant's neural activity changes from one turn-length interval to the next: higher values indicate greater fluctuations, and lower values indicate more stable activity.

We then compared partners' AVAR values to derive an "AVAR matching" score, using the absolute difference between partners' AVAR values followed by a negative-log transformation consistent with conventions in the complexity-matching literature BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 15 (Abney et al., 2014).

text.text: Higher values indicate more similar magnitudes of neural fluctuation between partners, and lower values indicate more differentiated dynamics.
Importantly, AVAR matching does not require partners' neural signals to rise and fall together at the same moments (the time-locked coordination is captured by IBS).
When linking neural and linguistic data, neural windows were shifted by 5 seconds to account for the hemodynamic delay (Tesler et al., 2023).

Consider two stylized forms of dance to clarify what AVAR and AVAR matching measure.
A waltz dancer might maintain a similar average movement intensity from one phrase to the next, producing low AVAR at the phrase scale.
A freestyle street dancer might alternate sharply between restrained and explosive phrases, producing high AVAR.
The distinction is not that waltz is regular and freestyle is unpredictable; it is that neighboring phrases differ less in the first example and more in the second.
The dyadic comparison then asks whether the two dancers exhibit similar amounts of phrase-to-phrase change.
Two steady dancers can be closely matched, as can two highly variable dancers; a highly variable dancer paired with a steady one would be less matched.
Matching therefore concerns the resemblance of the partners' dynamics, not the dynamics of either partner alone.
Throughout the analyses, we used dyad as the unit (N = 70 unless otherwise noted).

text.text: Across the 70 stranger dyads, conversations yielded 22,726 cross-speaker turn pairs, of which 11,100 (49%) met the criterion for substantive exchange.
Dyads produced an average of 159 substantive exchanges (SD = 64, range = 44-325), with a median of 146 exchanges per dyad.

H1: Linguistic Convergence Entropy Over Time H1 posed competing predictions from two theoretical traditions: entropy would decrease if strangers progressively aligned, but increase if they progressively broadened the semantic ground of the conversation.
Results supported the latter.
We tested this pattern both continuously over the course of the conversation and by comparing entropy across four conversation quarters.
Entropy increased over conversation time across all exchanges (p < .001) and substantive exchanges (p < .001).
text.formatted: Entropy increased over conversation time across all exchanges (p < .001) and substantive exchanges (p < .001).

text.text: The same pattern emerged when conversations were divided into quarters.

When each conversation was divided into four quarters, entropy differed significantly across quarters for all exchanges (F(3, 207) = 3.80, p = .011) and for substantive exchanges (F(3, 207) = 4.97, p = .002).

Entropy was significantly higher in the final quarter than in the first quarter both across all turn exchanges (t(69) = 2.27, p = .026) and when focusing on substantive exchanges (t(69) = 2.73, p = .008).
Results supported H1b over H1a, such that adjacent turns became less semantically predictable as conversations unfolded.
H2 predicted that favorable conversational experiences would be associated with two linguistic signatures: semantic alignment (indicated by lower entropy) and the amount of substantive exchange.
Results indicated that semantic alignment was not associated with selfreported conversational experience (all |rs| ≤ .12, all ps ≥ .34).

However, greater amount of substantive exchange was associated with greater perceived similarity (partial r = .28, p = .021), engagement (r = .27, p = .023), friendship potential (r = .26, p = .028), and liking (r = .25, p = .041).
Similarity, engagement, and friendship potential remained significant after falsediscovery-rate correction within the focal outcome family (qs = .047), while liking was marginal (q = .052).

Substantive exchange was not associated with felt depth itself (r = -.09, p = .45), BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 17 suggesting that reciprocal, contentful exchange tracked positive evaluations of the interaction rather than how deep the conversation felt (Figure 3A).
text.formatted: Substantive exchange was not associated with felt depth itself (r = -.09, p = .45), BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 17 suggesting that reciprocal, contentful exchange tracked positive evaluations of the interaction rather than how deep the conversation felt (Figure <ref type="figure">3A</ref>).

text.text: Thus, H2 was partially supported for substantive exchange, but not semantic alignment.
We then examined how the amount of substantive exchange differed by conversational depth, operationalized both by assigned prompt condition and by experienced depth (median split).

Dyads assigned shallow prompts accumulated more substantive exchanges (M = 184) than those assigned deep prompts (M = 132) (t(68) = 3.66, p < .001, d = 0.87); the same pattern emerged for experienced depth (Ms = 177 vs. 134) (t(68) = 2.91, p = .005, d = 0.70) (Figure 3B).
text.formatted: Dyads assigned shallow prompts accumulated more substantive exchanges (M = 184) than those assigned deep prompts (M = 132) (t(68) = 3.66, p < .001, d = 0.87); the same pattern emerged for experienced depth (Ms = 177 vs. 134) (t(68) = 2.91, p = .005, d = 0.70) (Figure <ref type="figure">3B</ref>).

text.text: The assigned conditions also differed in how talk was organized: deep-condition dyads produced longer turns (M = 17.2 vs.

14.3 tokens) (t(68) = 2.30, p = .024, d = 0.55), and fewer total language tokens overall (t(68) = 2.42, p = .018, d = 0.58), while the proportion of turn pairs meeting the substantive-exchange criterion did not differ (.50 vs. .53, p = .39).
Thus, the difference in the amount of substantive exchange appears to reflect how conversational contributions were organized rather than simply whether turns were substantive.

Depth did not moderate the associations of substantive exchange with friendship potential, similarity, or liking (interaction Fs(1, 66) ≤ 1.12, ps ≥ .29), and the associations were directionally positive within both shallow and deep conversations (e.g., liking within experienced-deep conversations: r = .38, p = .037).
However, engagement was the exception.
Even though participants assigned deep prompts reported greater engagement overall (M = 3.91 vs.

3.60) (t(68) = 2.14, p = .036, d = 0.51), substantive exchange was unrelated to engagement within deep conversations, whether depth was assigned (r = -.01, p = .97) or experienced (r = -.04, p = .81).
Within shallow conversations, greater substantive exchange was associated with substantially greater engagement under both operationalizations (assigned: r = .46, p = .004,
Figure 3C; experienced: r = .47, p = .002, Figure 3D).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">3C</ref>; experienced: r = .47, p = .002, Figure <ref type="figure">3D</ref>).

text.text: Accordingly, the exchange × depth interaction was significant for engagement under both assigned (F(1, 66) = 4.86, p = .031), and experienced depth (F(1, 66) = 4.88, p = .031), but not for the other relational evaluations.

A median split within the shallow condition illustrated the magnitude of this association: highexchange dyads reported greater engagement (M = 3.86) than low-exchange dyads (M = 3.33) (t(34) = 2.62, p = .013, d = 0.87) (Figure 3E).
text.formatted: A median split within the shallow condition illustrated the magnitude of this association: highexchange dyads reported greater engagement (M = 3.86) than low-exchange dyads (M = 3.33) (t(34) = 2.62, p = .013, d = 0.87) (Figure <ref type="figure">3E</ref>).

text.text: Deep prompts were engaging on their own.
With shallow prompts, engagement depended more on the exchange partners built, while relational evaluations tracked exchange regardless of depth.
H3 predicted that linguistic signatures are associated with interpersonal neural coordination.

We examined two linguistic measures (convergence entropy and amount of substantive exchanges) against two neural coordination measures: inter-brain synchrony (IBS; previously computed values from Miao et al. (2026)) and AVAR matching.
text.formatted: We examined two linguistic measures (convergence entropy and amount of substantive exchanges) against two neural coordination measures: inter-brain synchrony (IBS; previously computed values from <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Miao et al. (2026)</ref>) and AVAR matching.

text.text: IBS and AVAR matching were not interchangeable measures of coordination: within-network correlation ranged from r = -.24 to .31 (DMN r = -.24, p = .051; FPN r = -.05, p = .66; VAN r = -.04, p = .73; DAN r = .31, p = .033), corresponding to at most 9.4% shared variance.
Convergence entropy was unrelated to IBS across all networks (all ps ≥ .36).

In contrast, the amount of substantive exchanges was associated with greater IBS in the DMN (r = .29, p = .015), VAN (r = .32, p = .007), and FPN (r = .26, p = .028), with all three effects surviving Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across the four networks tested.
This association was not significant in the DAN (r = .16, p = .27).
Thus, greater inter-brain synchrony was associated with a larger amount of substantive exchanges, but not with greater semantic alignment between turns.
AVAR matching showed a different pattern.

In turn-level analyses, greater matching of partners' neural dynamics was associated with lower entropy, indicating greater semantic alignment, in the DMN (p = .007) and right TPJ (p = .008), with no comparable effects in other networks or regions.
Meanwhile, AVAR matching was not significantly associated with the amount of substantive exchanges (ps ≥ .053).

Overall, H3 was supported for the association between substantive exchanges and interbrain synchrony, with preliminary evidence that semantic alignment may instead relate to similarity in partners' turn-to-turn neural dynamics.
Conversation looks effortless but is cognitively demanding.

Conversation requires people to continuously comprehend a partner's contribution, anticipate what may come next, and formulate a response, all while pursuing interpersonal goals under real-time cognitive constraints (Berger, 1997; Gasiorek & Aune, 2021; Kellermann, 1992).
text.formatted: Conversation requires people to continuously comprehend a partner's contribution, anticipate what may come next, and formulate a response, all while pursuing interpersonal goals under real-time cognitive constraints <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Berger, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gasiorek & Aune, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Kellermann, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: This complexity is also reflected at the neural level.

Real-life conversation recruits not only the core language system but also broader brain networks involved in constructing meaning across context, mentalizing, and social cognition (Zada et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Real-life conversation recruits not only the core language system but also broader brain networks involved in constructing meaning across context, mentalizing, and social cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Zada et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Communication theories have therefore long treated alignment and adaptation as central to successful interaction (Giles et al., 1991), yet considerably less is known about how these processes actually unfold from one exchange to the next and how they relate to interpersonal outcomes (Solomon et al., 2021 (Solomon et al., , 2023)).
text.formatted: Communication theories have therefore long treated alignment and adaptation as central to successful interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Giles et al., 1991)</ref>, yet considerably less is known about how these processes actually unfold from one exchange to the next and how they relate to interpersonal outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Solomon et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Solomon et al., , 2023))</ref>.

text.text: This study examined this process across linguistic, experiential, and neural levels during first conversations between strangers.
Three findings emerged.
First, strangers did not become progressively more semantically predictable over the course of a 20-minute conversation.
Instead, adjacent turns broadened in semantic range over time (H1).

Second, how positively strangers experienced the conversation BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 20 was related not to their average level of semantic alignment, but to how much reciprocal and substantive exchange they accumulated.
For engagement, this relationship was even more pronounced in shallow conversations (H2).
Third, different linguistic signatures mapped onto distinct forms of neural coordination.

Substantive exchange was associated with inter-brain synchrony in the DMN, VAN, and FPN, whereas semantic alignment was associated with matching of turn-to-turn neural dynamics in the DMN and more specifically, the right TPJ (an anatomically defined region within our DMN coverage) (H3).

These findings suggest that conversational coordination should not be reduced to a single form of "alignment": how meaning develops, how much reciprocal and contentful exchange partners construct, and how their neural activity coordinates capture related but distinguishable aspects of interaction.

Together, the findings tell a story that conversation is skilled work built turn-by-turn: prompts are only the starting points of conversations, but engagement is co-constructed with reciprocal and substantive exchanges by the conversation partners themselves.
H1 qualifies a straightforward convergence account of initial interactions between strangers.

Communication accommodation theory conceptualizes convergence as interlocutors' mutual adaptation across communicative behaviors, often in ways that reduce social distance (Giles et al., 1991; Soliz et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Communication accommodation theory conceptualizes convergence as interlocutors' mutual adaptation across communicative behaviors, often in ways that reduce social distance <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Giles et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Soliz et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: If this process manifested as progressively increasing semantic similarity, adjacent turns should have become more predictable as strangers talk.
Instead, entropy increased: strangers moved from relatively constrained early exchanges toward a broader semantic range as they got to know each other.

Instead, this trajectory resonates with social penetration theory, which proposes that relationship development involves an expansion in breadth and depth of self-disclosure during conversation (Altman & Taylor, 1973).
text.formatted: Instead, this trajectory resonates with social penetration theory, which proposes that relationship development involves an expansion in breadth and depth of self-disclosure during conversation <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Altman & Taylor, 1973)</ref>.

text.text: Although social penetration theory primarily describes BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 21 changes that unfold over longer-term relationship development, the present findings suggest that a related process may already be observable within a single initial conversation.

As strangers establish enough common ground to sustain the interaction, successive turns may become less constrained by the immediately preceding content, allowing the conversation to move into a wider range of meanings and topics.
Convergence, in other words, need not imply that conversational content becomes progressively narrower or more redundant.
This pattern does not imply an absence of accommodation.
Rather, it suggests that accommodation during conversation need not take the form of progressively narrowing semantic content.
Convergence can occur across multiple dimensions (such as in timing and other features of interaction), even while partners introduce increasingly varied ideas.
The process model of creating understanding describes conversation as requiring both prediction and the continual updating of situation models (Gasiorek & Aune, 2021).
text.formatted: The process model of creating understanding describes conversation as requiring both prediction and the continual updating of situation models <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gasiorek & Aune, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Some predictability is necessary for partners to understand and respond to one another, but perfectly predictable conversation would leave little room for new information.

The increase in entropy observed here may therefore reflect a balance crucial to developing good conversation: turns ought to be sufficiently connected to what came before to be understood while progressively opening new semantic ground that moves the interaction forward.
H2 connects linguistic signatures with self-reported experiences of the interaction.
Average entropy was unrelated to participants' evaluations of the conversation.
By contrast, dyads that accumulated more substantive exchanges tended to report greater engagement, liking, similarity, and friendship potential.
This distinction is theoretically informative: semantic similarity alone was not what differentiated positively experienced conversations.
Notably, the moderation by conversational depth further clarifies this pattern.
Deep prompts produced greater engagement on average, but within deep conversations, accumulating more substantive exchanges did not predict additional engagement.
The relationship was instead concentrated among shallow conversations, whether depth was defined experimentally or by participants' subjective experience.

These results suggest that deep questions may relatively directly provide conversational material that supports engagement; but when the material itself is shallow, the interaction appears to depend more on what partners construct from it.
A question about the weather can still produce an engaging conversation, but doing so may require partners to repeatedly take up, elaborate, and return substantive contributions to one another.

This finding complements a dynamic dyadic systems (DDS) perspective and conversational-motif analysis on interpersonal communication, which locates the consequential structure of conversation in the unfolding exchange between partners rather than in isolated messages or whole-conversation summaries (Solomon et al., 2021 (Solomon et al., , 2023 (Solomon et al., , 2025)).
text.formatted: This finding complements a dynamic dyadic systems (DDS) perspective and conversational-motif analysis on interpersonal communication, which locates the consequential structure of conversation in the unfolding exchange between partners rather than in isolated messages or whole-conversation summaries <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Solomon et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Solomon et al., , 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Solomon et al., , 2025))</ref>.

text.text: DDS treats a turn not as an isolated behavior but as both a response to what preceded it and a stimulus for what follows, such that interaction emerges through sequences of mutually contingent contributions.
Our measure of substantive exchange captures one simple feature of this process: how often adjacent turns contain reciprocal and substantial contributions from both partners.

Unlike conversational-motif approaches, which distinguish recurring sequences based on the functions and linguistic characteristics of turns, substantive exchange does not identify what kind of interaction is occurring.
Instead, it provides a scalable measure of how much reciprocal, contentful back-and-forth accumulates over a conversation.
The present findings suggest that even this relatively simple property of turn-to-turn organization may be consequential for how strangers experience an interaction.
While the substantive exchange measure captures one important form of interaction, it should not be treated as a comprehensive measure of meaningful engagement.

Conversation analysis has long emphasized that the function of a turn depends on its position within a larger sequence, and that interaction can be highly coordinated without symmetrical verbal contributions (Sacks et al., 1974; Schegloff, 2007).
text.formatted: Conversation analysis has long emphasized that the function of a turn depends on its position within a larger sequence, and that interaction can be highly coordinated without symmetrical verbal contributions <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Sacks et al., 1974;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Schegloff, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Storytelling is a clear example: one speaker may hold the floor across extended turns while the recipient contributes brief acknowledgments or backchannels that are interactionally consequential but fall below our five-token threshold.
Our measure therefore privileges reciprocal, contentful back-and-forth while underrepresenting other forms of sequence organization.
This limitation may be particularly relevant to the deep-prompt condition, where participants produced fewer and longer turns, consistent with more extended telling-and-listening sequences.

Because we did not formally distinguish storytelling, backchanneling, or other sequential structures, we cannot determine whether such patterns account for the weaker relationship between substantive exchange and engagement in deep conversations.
Future work could combine scalable quantitative measures with conversation-analytic or motif-based approaches to sequence organization.

With the support of recent development of dynamic data visualization dashboards such as DIMS (Miao et al., 2025), this allows different forms of interaction (i.e. reciprocal exchange, extended telling, active listening, and others) to be identified rather than collapsed into a single measure.
text.formatted: With the support of recent development of dynamic data visualization dashboards such as DIMS <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Miao et al., 2025)</ref>, this allows different forms of interaction (i.e. reciprocal exchange, extended telling, active listening, and others) to be identified rather than collapsed into a single measure.

text.text: H3 extends this dyadic account beyond language.
Substantive exchange was associated with time-locked inter-brain synchrony, whereas semantic alignment showed an association with similarity in partners' turn-to-turn neural dynamics.

The key point is therefore not simply that conversation partners' brains coordinate, but that different forms of neural coordination appear to BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 24 map onto different features of the interaction.

Inter-brain synchrony captures whether partners' neural activity co-fluctuates at corresponding moments, whereas AVAR matching captures similarity in the magnitude of turn-to-turn neural change without requiring the signals to move in lockstep.
This distinction may be especially relevant for conversation, where partners alternate between speaking, listening, interpreting, and responding.

Similarity in the dynamics of those processes may therefore capture forms of interpersonal coordination that conventional synchrony measures miss, broadening the methodological toolkit for studying naturally unfolding interaction.
The recurrence of the DMN and right TPJ across analyses is also theoretically suggestive.

Prior work in this sample linked IBS in DMN and right TPJ to felt interpersonal connection (Miao et al., 2026), while the present analyses connect it to both reciprocal exchange and semantic alignment through different neural metrics.
text.formatted: Prior work in this sample linked IBS in DMN and right TPJ to felt interpersonal connection <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Miao et al., 2026)</ref>, while the present analyses connect it to both reciprocal exchange and semantic alignment through different neural metrics.

text.text: This convergence is consistent with an important role for mentalizing-related systems in conversation.
More broadly, the study advances a dynamic dyadic approach by using the conversational turn as a common unit for linking linguistic and neural processes.

This moves analysis closer to the interaction itself: rather than relying primarily on transcripts or post-conversation summaries, contemporary recording and computational methods make it possible to align multiple streams of interaction data (including language, self-reported experience, and neural activity) within the unfolding conversation.

Such multimodal analysis can reveal how different forms of coordination emerge together, or diverge, from one exchange to the next (Solomon et al., 2021 (Solomon et al., , 2023 (Solomon et al., , 2025)).
text.formatted: Such multimodal analysis can reveal how different forms of coordination emerge together, or diverge, from one exchange to the next <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Solomon et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Solomon et al., , 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Solomon et al., , 2025))</ref>.

text.text: A central implication is that interpersonal coordination is not a unitary phenomenon.
Semantic alignment, reciprocal participation, time-locked neural synchrony, and similarity in BUILDING CONNECTION THROUGH CONVERSATION 25 neural dynamics did not simply rise and fall together.

Their divergence is theoretically useful rather than problematic, suggesting that successful conversation can involve multiple, partly independent forms of coordination operating at different levels and timescales.
Multimodal approaches can therefore refine communication theory by specifying what is coordinated during interaction, rather than treating alignment as a single underlying property of the dyad.

For example, combining scalable computational measures with sequence-sensitive approaches, facilitated by dynamic data dashboards such as DIMS (Miao et al., 2025), would allow future research to distinguish reciprocal dialogue, extended telling, active listening, and other conversational organizations rather than treating one structure as representative of engagement as a whole.

text.text: Together, findings across linguistic, experiential, and neural dimensions portray conversation as skilled work built turn by turn.
Prompts may provide the starting point, but they do not determine whether an interaction becomes engaging.
Especially when prompts were shallow, engagement was associated with the reciprocal and substantive exchanges that partners constructed together over the course of the conversation.
At the same time, strangers did not simply converge toward increasingly similar semantic content; their conversations broadened semantically as they unfolded.

The brain registered both sides of the story: inter-brain synchrony tracked the accumulation of substantive exchange, while matching of turn-to-turn neural dynamics showed preliminary links to semantic alignment.
Conversation is thus co-constructed, contribution by contribution, by the people taking part in it.

Finally, research on communication as a process of creating shared understanding highlights the roles of prediction and alignment and suggests that different aspects of conversation may be reflected in distinct forms of neural coordination.
Integrating these perspectives, we test the following hypotheses.
H1a: Semantic alignment increases over the course of the interaction.
H1b: Semantic alignment decreases over the course of the interaction.
Semantic alignment and substantive exchange are positively associated with favorable communication experiences.
Neural coordination is positively associated with semantic alignment and substantive exchange.
